chapter.title: Agent, chatbot, or plain script: picking the right tool

cards.body:
You have three kinds of help in the office. A photocopier does the same thing every time and never thinks. A colleague across the desk answers your question, then you go do the thing yourself. The intern takes the whole task and works through it alone while you do something else.

A script is the photocopier. A chatbot is the colleague. An agent is the intern. Most mistakes with AI come from handing the intern a photocopier job, or a job where one slip costs real money.

cards.title: Three tools, three questions
cards.body:
A script is a fixed list of steps a person wrote once. It runs the same way every time and never decides anything. A chatbot answers one question, then stops; you do all the acting. An agent runs the loop from chapter 2: it picks a step, runs it, reads the result, and picks again until the goal is done.

To choose between them, ask 3 questions about the task.

Question 1: do I know the exact steps before I start? If you can write them as a numbered list now, and the list never changes, you want a script. No model needed at all.

Question 2: does each step need judgement? Judgement means reading what came back and choosing what to do next. If yes, a script cannot do it. It has to be a chatbot or an agent.

Question 3: how bad is a mistake, and can I undo it? This decides who does the acting. If a slip is cheap or reversible, let the agent act. If a slip is costly or permanent, keep the acting with you: use a chatbot, or an agent that must ask before the risky step.

cards.prompt: You have 500 photos named IMG_0001.jpg to IMG_0500.jpg. You want them renamed to trip-0001.jpg through trip-0500.jpg. Which tool fits?

options.text: An agent, because 500 is a lot of steps
A script, because the steps are known before you start
A chatbot, so you can rename each one as it tells you

whyNot.a: That's confusing many steps with judgement: the agent loop is for steps you can't list in advance, and here every step is identical.
whyNot.c: That's the chatbot for a task that needs no judgement: you would type 500 times for a job a script finishes in 1 second.

cards.reteach: Ask question 1 first. Can you write the steps now, and will they stay the same for all 500 files? Yes: take the number from the old name, put it after 'trip-'. A fixed list of steps is a script. Models only earn their cost when some step needs a decision.

cards.title: Researching a laptop
cards.body:
You want a laptop for video editing under a set budget. You cannot list the steps in advance: you don't know which reviews exist, which models are in stock, or which price pages are stale. Question 1 says no script.

Each step needs judgement. After one search the agent must decide: open this review, or skip it? Is this price current? Question 2 says a model is needed.

A mistake is cheap. The worst case is a weak recommendation, and you still click buy yourself. Question 3 says let it act. Verdict: an agent with the search and read-page tools from chapter 3, a step cap of about 30, and no payment tool.

cards.title: Sorting email, and mixed tasks
cards.body:
Sorting email looks like one task but the 3 questions split it. Deciding which emails matter needs judgement, so a model is involved. Putting a label on an email is reversible; deleting or replying is not.

So the answer is an agent with two speeds. It may label freely. Before any delete or any reply, it must stop and get a human yes, the guardrail from chapter 6. Question 3 does not pick one tool for the whole job. It picks who acts at each risky step.

Many real tasks are mixed like this. Split them. Use a script for the fixed part and an agent only for the part that needs judgement. When you are unsure, start with the chatbot: it is cheaper, and you stay in the loop until you trust the task.

cards.prompt: A friend runs a small shop and has 40 customer emails to answer. Each one asks something different. Which setup applies the 3 questions correctly?

options.text: An agent that reads each email and sends its reply straight away
A script that sends the same thank-you reply to all 40
An agent that drafts each reply, and the friend clicks send on every one

whyNot.a: That skips question 3: a wrong reply sent to a customer cannot be unsent, so the send step needs a human yes.
whyNot.b: That's the script for a job that needs judgement: each email asks something different, so no fixed list of steps fits.

cards.reteach: Run the three questions. Steps known in advance? No, each email is different. Judgement per step? Yes, so a model. Mistake costly and permanent? Yes, a bad reply reaches a real customer. So the model does the thinking and drafting, and the human keeps the one action that cannot be undone: send.

cards.body: The common mistake is reaching for an agent because agents are exciting, when a script would do. Agents cost more per run, are slower, and can wander off into the failure types from chapter 5. The test for spotting it: if you can write the steps as a numbered list before starting, and the list is the same every time, you have described a script. Build that instead.

cards.prompt: You are choosing between the three tools. Which answer points to a plain script?

options.text: "The steps are the same every time and I can list them right now."
"Each step depends on what the last step found."
"A mistake would be costly and hard to undo."

whyNot.b: That's question 2, judgement at each step: it rules a script out and points to a chatbot or agent.
whyNot.c: That's question 3, cost of a mistake: it decides who holds the risky action, not whether a script is enough.

cards.reteach: Question 1 is the script question. A known, unchanging list of steps means no decisions are needed, so no model is needed. Questions 2 and 3 only come into play once the path is unknown and something has to be judged along the way.

cards.body: Write 3 tasks from your week on paper. Next to each, answer the 3 questions with one word. Circle script, chatbot, or agent. Keep the paper for day 14.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now run any task through the 3-question test and say whether it deserves a script, a chatbot, or an agent, with the reason.
